attributes.nuance_translation: A common way to indicate that (B) will be done without doing (A).

attributes.body:
There are two primary ways in which ないで is used with verbs in Japanese. The first is to express 'without doing (A), (B)'. The second is to request that someone 'not do (A)'. We will examine the first in this write-up.

ないで is a combination of the auxiliary verb ない, and the particle で. Due to this, で keeps its standard meaning of 'with/by', in relation to 'not' doing something.

When ないで is used to express that '(A) has not been done before doing (B)', this is usually contrary to some kind of expectation. Because of this, ないで is often used to express something that may be surprising to the listener.

Caution

Be careful of the following two structures:

(A) ないで (B) - Without doing (A), (B).

(A) なくて (B) - Without doing (A), (B).

Technically, these two constructions share a similar meaning. However, in modern Japanese ないで is used more frequently when the (B) action is being highlighted as being done without (A). On the other hand, なくて is used when (A) is being given as a reason for why something else was/wasn't done.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar
[AIAIJ] An Integrated Approach to Intermediate Japanese

attributes.description: なくて vs ないで

attributes.body: Though these two phrases appear similar in form, both suggesting 'without doing', they differ in that ともなく・ともなしに is used figuratively to express that the action was performed, but in an absentminded manner, or ‘without even so much as the intention of doing (A), (B)’, e.g. 見るともなく見ていたら 'as I was absentmindedly looking...' whereas ないで literally means that action was not performed, e.g. 見ないでやる 'do without looking'.

first_relatable.title: ともなく・ともなしに
first_relatable.meaning: Absentmindedly, Mindlessly, Unconsciously, Without paying attention

attributes.body: ないで and なくて are both negative connecting forms, but with different uses. ないで is used in negative requests or to mean 'without doing' something, e.g. 食べないでください ('Please don't eat it.'). and 朝ご飯を食べないで学校に行った ('I went to school without eating breakfast.'). なくて connects clauses to describe reasons or states, similar to 'and', e.g. 高くなくて便利です ('It's not expensive, and it's convenient.').

ないで and なくて are both connecting forms of ない, but with different uses. ないで is used in negative requests or to mean 'without doing' something, e.g. 食べないでください ('Please don't eat it.') and 朝ご飯を食べないで学校に行った ('I went to school without eating breakfast.'). なくて can express a reason or cause, e.g. 行けなくて残念でした ('I couldn't go, which was disappointing.').

second_relatable.title: なくて
second_relatable.meaning: Not ~ and, Not so, Because not (Examples)

attributes.body: ないで and ずに both express the idea of 'without doing (A)' and are used in similar ways. For example, 朝ご飯を食べないで学校に行った and 朝ご飯を食べずに学校に行った both mean 'I went to school without eating breakfast.', but ずに has a slightly more formal or literary tone, while ないで is more conversational. Unlike ないで, ずに cannot be used as a negative request form to say 'Don't (A).'.

The dictionary/non-past form of a verb + な expresses a blunt command not to do something. Similarly, ないで attached to the negative stem of a verb is a more casual and gentle request. For example, するな is a strong way of saying 'Don't do it!' while しないで is a softer, more casual way of saying '[Please] don't do it.'

〜てください is a polite way to say 'Please do (something),' as in 食べてください ('Please eat'). Its negative form, 〜ないで, means 'Don't do (something),' as in 食べないで ('Don't eat'). To make this negative request polite, simply add ください, as in 食べないでください means 'Please don't eat.'

なさい is a firm but polite command form, often used by those in authority (like teachers or parents) toward subordinates. In contrast, ないで is a casual way to ask someone not to do something, e.g. 行かないで ('Don't go.'). It is typically used among close friends or family.

The ないで form combines a verb in the negative with で, and has two common uses: (1) to make a negative request, e.g. 食べないで ('Don't eat it.'), and (2) to express 'without doing' something, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べないで出かけた ('I went out without eating dinner.').

ないでください is a polite way to ask someone not to do something. The shorter form, ないで, is more casual and typically used with close friends or family. While ないでください is appropriate for strangers or people of equal status, ないで has a softer, more informal tone. Adding the sentence-ending particle ね (e.g. 食べないでね) makes the request even gentler and more caring.
